draft.title: Limiting reagents
card: Reactants combine in the ratio given by the balanced equation. In most reactions one reactant is used up before the others.
the reactant that runs out first. The reaction stops when it is gone, so it sets how much product can form.
a reactant that is left over when the reaction stops.

To find the limiting reagent, change each amount to moles and compare it with the ratio in the equation. For 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, 2 mol of H2 needs 1 mol of O2. If there is less O2 than that, O2 is limiting.
draft.remember: The limiting reagent runs out first and sets the amount of product.

a.q: In a reaction, one reactant is used up and the reaction stops. Some of the other reactant is left over. What does the leftover reactant show?
opts: It is in excess, and the used up reactant was limiting
It is limiting, and the used up reactant was in excess
Both reactants were present in the exact ratio
The reaction did not follow the balanced equation
a.why: The reaction stops when one reactant runs out, so that one is limiting. The reactant left over is in excess. It is not limiting, because it did not stop the reaction.
a.clue: Which reactant ran out and stopped the reaction?

b.q: Hydrogen reacts with oxygen: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. A flask holds 4 mol of H2 and 1 mol of O2. Which statement is correct?
opts: O2 is limiting, and 2 mol of H2O can form
H2 is limiting, and 4 mol of H2O can form
O2 is limiting, and 1 mol of H2O can form
H2 is in excess, and 4 mol of H2O can form
b.why: 1 mol of O2 needs only 2 mol of H2, and there is 4 mol, so O2 runs out first and is limiting. The ratio of O2 to H2O is 1 to 2, so 2 mol of H2O forms. H2 is not limiting, even though its amount is larger in number than the O2.
b.clue: Use the equation's ratio to find how much H2 1 mol of O2 needs.

a.best: It is in excess, and the used up reactant was limiting

b.best: O2 is limiting, and 2 mol of H2O can form

problems.detail: The question asks how much H2O forms. The card says the limiting reagent sets the amount of product, but its worked example only shows how to find the limiting reagent. It never shows using the reactant-to-product ratio (1 O2 : 2 H2O) to work out the amount of product, so students must take a step the card does not teach.

check.summary: The facts and both answers are correct. One minor issue: question b asks for the amount of product, but the card never shows how to use the equation's ratio to work that out.

proposal.title: Limiting reagents
card: the reactant that runs out first. The reaction stops when it is gone, so it sets how much product can form.
a reactant that is left over when the reaction stops.

Reactants combine in the ratio in the balanced equation. To find the limiting reagent, change each amount to moles and compare. In 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, 2 mol of H2 needs 1 mol of O2, so if there is less O2 than that, O2 is limiting.
Then use the moles of the limiting reagent and the equation's ratio to find the product. Here 1 mol of O2 makes 2 mol of H2O, so 0.5 mol of O2 makes 1 mol of H2O.
proposal.remember: Find which reactant runs out first, then use its moles and the ratio to find the product.
